securityInformation.title: Bypassing enforce mountable secrets policy imposed by the ServiceAccount admission plugin
securityInformation.description:
A security issue was discovered in Kubernetes where users may be able to launch containers that bypass the mountable secrets policy enforced by the ServiceAccount admission plugin when using ephemeral containers. The policy ensures pods running with a service account may only reference secrets specified in the service account's secrets field. Kubernetes clusters are only affected if the ServiceAccount admission plugin and the `kubernetes.io/enforce-mountable-secrets` annotation are used together with ephemeral containers.

**Note**: This only impacts the cluster if the ServiceAccount admission plugin is used (most cluster should have this on by default as recommended in https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/admission-controllers/#serviceaccount), the `kubernetes.io/enforce-mountable-secrets` annotation is used by a service account (this annotation is not added by default), and Pods are using ephemeral containers.

bugOrRegression.description: Added a method `StreamWithContext` to `remotecommand.Executor` to support cancelable SPDY executor stream.
bugOrRegression.author: arkbriar
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Add a method `StreamWithContext` to remotecommand.Executor to support cancelable SPDY executor stream.

enrichment.problem: The existing remotecommand.Executor interface lacked a way to cancel an ongoing SPDY exec stream, making it difficult to gracefully stop exec sessions via context cancellation.
enrichment.affected: Clients that use the remotecommand.Executor (e.g., kubectl exec, custom tooling built on client-go) and any workloads that rely on exec over SPDY.
enrichment.fix: Introduced a new `StreamWithContext` method on the `remotecommand.Executor` interface, allowing callers to provide a context that can be cancelled to stop the SPDY executor stream.
enrichment.impact: Users of `kubectl exec` and other tools built on client-go can now cleanly abort exec sessions, preventing hung streams and improving resource cleanup and user experience.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed relative CPU priority for pods where containers explicitly request zero cpu by giving the lowest priority instead of falling back to the cpu limit to avoid possible cpu starvation of other pods.
bugOrRegression.author: waynepeking348
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: fix relative cpu priority for pods where containers explicitly request zero cpu by giving the lowest priority instead of falling back to the cpu limit to avoid possible cpu starvation of other pods

enrichment.problem: Pods with containers that explicitly request 0 CPU were given a relative CPU priority based on their CPU limit, which could give them higher priority than intended and risk starving other pods of CPU time.
enrichment.affected: Pods that specify a zero CPU request for one or more containers; other pods on the same node could be impacted by CPU starvation.
enrichment.fix: The relative CPU priority calculation now treats containers with a zero CPU request as the lowest priority, ignoring the limit for priority determination, thereby preventing unintended CPU starvation.
enrichment.impact: Ensures fair CPU distribution on nodes, avoiding scenarios where zero‑request pods monopolize CPU resources and improving overall workload stability.

bugOrRegression.description: Removed of raising an error when setting an annotation with the same value, just ignore it.
bugOrRegression.author: zigarn
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Do not raise an error when setting an annotation with the same value, just ignore it.

enrichment.affected: Users invoking kubectl to set annotations on resources; automation that reapplies the same manifest.
enrichment.fix: The CLI now silently ignores a no‑op annotation update (same key/value) instead of raising an error.
enrichment.impact: Idempotent scripts and manual workflows no longer fail on redundant annotation updates, reducing friction and improving user experience.

bugOrRegression.description: kubectl apply: warning that kubectl will ignore no-namespaced resource `pv & namespace` in a future release if the namespace is specified and allowlist is not specified.
bugOrRegression.author: pacoxu

enrichment.problem: kubectl apply currently allows specifying a namespace for cluster‑scoped resources like PersistentVolume and Namespace, but in a future release those resources will be ignored unless an allowlist is provided. Users may be unaware and experience silent failures.

enrichment.fix: kubectl now emits a warning when a namespace is supplied for a non‑namespaced resource without an allowlist, alerting users that such resources will be ignored in a future version.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed bug in `kubectl rollout history` where only the latest revision was displayed when a specific revision was requested and an output format was specified.

issueContext.title: Rollout history doesn't show the revision when output format is used
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

If you use `kubectl rollout history --revision=100` you get the pod spec at revision 100. 

Everything is correct. However, if you add the `-o json` or `-o yaml` on the command, you just get the latest deployment, and not the revision you specified.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected to get the deployment spec of the revision I specified, or at least some json representation of what I see without the `-o json`

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

create a deployment. Update the deployment `image` using `kubectl apply -f mydeployment.yaml` a couple times. 
Run `kubectl rollout history deployment/my-deployment --revision 1`

Then add the `-o json` at the end. Compare the image tag in both versions. They won't be the same. When you add `-o json` you get the latest revision instead.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>

</details>

# paste output here

enrichment.affected: kubectl users requesting deployment rollout history with `--revision` and `-o json`/`-o yaml`.
enrichment.fix: The CLI logic was updated to correctly apply the revision filter even when an output format is specified, ensuring the requested revision's pod spec is returned in the requested format.

bugOrRegression.description: Updated `kube-proxy` to restart in case it detects that the Node assigned `pod.Spec.PodCIDRs` have changed.
bugOrRegression.author: aojea
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: kube-proxy, will restart in case it detects that the Node assigned pod.Spec.PodCIDRs have changed

issueContext.title: kube-proxy in LocalModeNodeCIDR mode may cache stale Node.PodCIDR if the Node object is recreated
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

If `LocalModeNodeCIDR` is true, kube-proxy reads the `Node.PodCIDR` value and uses it to determine whether or not traffic is local to the Node.

In certain cases (e.g. when kube-proxy runs before the Node information has been completely updated), it is possible for kube-proxy to read and store a stale `PodCIDR` value. This will cause kube-proxy to route traffic incorrectly as the local traffic determination is no longer correct.

Note: PodCIDR is immutable once set but it is possible to delete and recreate the Node object to get into this state. (yes, this can happen)

/sig network

### What did you expect to happen?

kube-proxy should detect this state and reconfigure/restart with the newly updated `PodCIDR`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Recreate the Node object with a different PodCIDR after kube-proxy has started on the Node.

### Kubernetes version

Impacts all current versions that support `LocalModeNodeCIDR`

### Cloud provider

<details>
Observed for GCE preemptible/spot VMs, but is a generic problem.
</details>

enrichment.problem: When kube-proxy runs with LocalModeNodeCIDR enabled, it may cache a stale Node.PodCIDR if the Node object is recreated with a different CIDR. This leads to incorrect local‑traffic determination and misrouting of pod traffic.
enrichment.affected: Nodes running kube-proxy with LocalModeNodeCIDR enabled, especially when the Node object is deleted and recreated with a new PodCIDR (e.g., GCE preemptible/spot VMs).
enrichment.fix: kube-proxy now monitors the Node's pod.Spec.PodCIDRs and triggers a restart when the CIDR changes, ensuring it reloads the updated CIDR and restores correct traffic routing.
enrichment.impact: Ensures that traffic is correctly classified as local or remote after a node's PodCIDR changes, preventing connectivity issues for services and pods that rely on accurate network routing.

bugOrRegression.description: kubeadm: added `show-join-command` as a new separate phase at the end of `kubeadm init`. You can skip printing the join information by using `kubeadm init --skip-phases=show-join-command`. Executing only this phase on demand will throw an error because the phase needs dependencies such as bootstrap tokens to be pre-populated.
bugOrRegression.author: SataQiu
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: kubeadm: "show-join-command" has been added as a new separate phase at the end of "kubeadm init". You can skip printing the join information by using "kubeadm init --skip-phases=show-join-command". Executing only this phase on demand will throw an error because the phase needs dependencies such as bootstrap tokens to be pre-populated.

enrichment.problem: kubeadm init always printed the join command at the end and there was no way to skip this output. Additionally, there was no dedicated phase to generate the join command, making it impossible to run that logic independently.
enrichment.affected: Administrators using `kubeadm init` who want to control whether the join command is printed, and scripts that may invoke kubeadm phases directly.
enrichment.fix: Introduced a new "show-join-command" phase that runs at the end of `kubeadm init`. Users can now skip printing the join information with `--skip-phases=show-join-command`. The phase relies on existing bootstrap token data, so invoking it alone will error unless those dependencies are pre‑populated.
enrichment.impact: Cluster administrators gain finer control over the init workflow, allowing them to suppress join command output when not needed. They also receive a clear error when attempting to run the phase without required bootstrap tokens, preventing silent failures.

bugOrRegression.description: Reverted regression that prevented `client-go` latency metrics to be reported with a template URL to avoid label cardinality.
bugOrRegression.author: aanm
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Revert 1.24 regression that prevented client-go latency metrics to be reported with a template URL to avoid label cardinality.

issueContext.title: Regression in client-go >= v1.24.0 metrics lead to explosion in label cardinality
issueContext.body: ### What happened? Hello, we have been using client-go [`LatencyMetric` interface](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/v1.12.0/vendor/k8s.io/client-go/tools/metrics/metrics.go#L40-L43) to measure the latency for all client-go traffic from Cilium to kube-apiserver. We have [recently found out](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/20810) that since v1.24.0 the URL path is no longer aggregated in a way that this cardinality would no longer happen as presented in the following image: It seems this functionality was removed as a part of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/106911 as it seems that PR only took into account that users of the `LatencyMetric` would only be using it to measure latency to a particular host and not for a particular URL path as we are doing in [here](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/v1.12.0/pkg/k8s/watchers/watcher.go#L287-L289). Would it be reasonable to revert commit https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/106911/commits/bebf5a608f68523fc430a44f6db26b16022dc862 in order to fix this regression? Thanks cc @wojtek-t @aojea @liggitt

enrichment.problem: A regression introduced in client-go v1.24.0 stopped latency metrics from using a templated URL, causing each request path to be a separate Prometheus label. This led to massive label cardinality explosion, breaking observability for users relying on client-go LatencyMetric (e.g., Cilium).
enrichment.affected: Any component or third‑party controller (e.g., Cilium) that uses client-go LatencyMetric to measure API request latency. The regression affected clusters that scrape these metrics with Prometheus or similar systems.
enrichment.fix: Revert the change that removed URL templating in client-go’s LatencyMetric implementation (reverting PR #106911). This restores aggregation of latency metrics by a template URL, preventing high cardinality.
enrichment.impact: Metrics collection for client-go traffic works again without overwhelming metric storage back‑ends. Users can safely monitor request latency to the kube‑apiserver, and clusters avoid performance degradation or crashes caused by excessive metric cardinality.

bugOrRegression.description: kube-proxy no longer falls back from ipvs mode to iptables mode if you ask it to do ipvs but the system is not correctly configured. Instead, it will just exit with an error.
bugOrRegression.author: danwinship

issueContext.title: kube-proxy should report events when the proxier failovers
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

kube-proxy should report k8s events of critical cases instead of just logging, e.g., kube-proxy failovers to iptables proxier when it should be running ipvs proxier, see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.24.3/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_others.go#L588

There might be other critical cases need sysadmin's attention, maybe we should check everywhere.

### Why is this needed?

The background is: we recently had kube-proxy’s ipvs scheduling algorithm changed, but one of the nodes didn’t have the corresponding kernel module. When the kube-proxy agent restarts, it failed to enable ipvs proxier, and failovered to iptables proxier. As a result, the ipvs rules and iptables rules are mixed together, causing network issues. I think this kind of failover is rather important, should be reported as k8s events.

enrichment.problem: kube-proxy silently fell back from ipvs mode to iptables mode when the node lacked proper ipvs kernel modules or configuration, leading to mixed ipvs/iptables rules and network connectivity issues, with no clear event or error reported.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using kube-proxy in ipvs mode on nodes that lack the required kernel modules or proper ipvs configuration; workloads relying on Service load balancing on those nodes.
enrichment.fix: The fallback behavior has been removed. When ipvs mode cannot be enabled, kube-proxy now exits with an error instead of automatically switching to iptables mode.
enrichment.impact: Prevents hidden network failures caused by mixed rule sets, making misconfiguration obvious and easier to diagnose. Operators must ensure correct ipvs setup or handle the error, improving cluster reliability.

This means that any watch cache metrics related to CRDs show them as Unstructured, which is misleading; and all log messages from the watch cache code only reference Unstructured instead of the specific CRD.

### What did you expect to happen?

Watch cache metrics and log messages would indicate the CRD type

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create some CRDs
2. Look at metrics / log messages related to watch cache

### Anything else we need to know?

The watch cache code relies on reflection to get the type of the object. This is where everything CRD related collapses to `*unstructured.Unstructured`. 

When the cacher is being created...

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bddb4ec08ee76c98a04cc857d346fd80d44abd8f/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go#L56-L68

we have the `storageConfig`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bddb4ec08ee76c98a04cc857d346fd80d44abd8f/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go#L38

which knows about the `GroupResource`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bddb4ec08ee76c98a04cc857d346fd80d44abd8f/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/storagebackend/config.go#L104

We could modify all the cacher-related structs to store the groupResource, and use that for metrics/logging, instead of the reflected object type.

C:\> w

enrichment.problem: Watch cache metrics and log messages treated all CustomResourceDefinition objects as *unstructured.Unstructured, so metrics and logs displayed the generic unstructured type instead of the actual CRD resource and group.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that run CustomResourceDefinitions and rely on watch cache metrics or logs for monitoring and debugging. Users inspecting apiserver logs or Prometheus metrics for CRDs were seeing them as unstructured.
enrichment.fix: The watch cache now keys log messages and metrics by `<resource>.<group>` rather than the Go struct type. Built‑in resources (e.g., Pod) are shown as 'pods', and CRD resources are displayed with their proper resource name and group.

`statusStrategy#ValidateUpdate` doesn't do the same embedded resource and x-kubernetes-list-type "map" and "set" invariant validation that happens in custom resource create/update validation.

bugOrRegression.description: Protobuf serialization of metav1.MicroTime timestamps (used in `Lease` and `Event` API objects) has been corrected to truncate to microsecond precision, to match the documented behavior and JSON/YAML serialization. Any existing persisted data is truncated to microsecond when read from etcd.
bugOrRegression.author: haoruan

issueContext.title: MicroTime marshalled at different precision for json and proto
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Found some error logs when sending series events to apiserver:
```
eventTime: Invalid value: 2022-08-19 16:00:45.305977 +0800 CST: field is immutable
``` 
seems the later eventTime differed from the first one in series events

After investigation, I found the problem was in the marshal.
MicroTime is supposed to work on microsecond level precision, but init with nanosecond level precision, in this case, `MarshalJSON` generates microsecond level precision data and `Marshal` generates nanosecond level precision, so when unmarshalled, the new time is not considered the exactly same as the original time (they are different at nanosecond level)

### What did you expect to happen?

MicroTime marshal should work at same precision for json and proto, so unmarshal can generate the exactly same MicroTime

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```go

issueContext.title: Using exec auth in kubectl triggers one connection per applied/described object
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Switching from the gcp auth provider to the exec auth provider in 1.25 made `kubectl apply` requests which previously made a single connection to the API server make one connection per applied object.

If enough items are applied, the connections can start to fail because of ephemeral port exhaustion

/kind bug
/milestone v1.25
/sig auth cli api-machinery

### What did you expect to happen?

Switching to the exec auth plugin would allow commands that previously worked to continue to work

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reproducer integration test at https://github.com/liggitt/kubernetes/commits/exec-auth-reproducer demonstrating one transport (and therefore a new connection) for each item in an applied file when using exec auth

on that branch:
```
go test ./test/integration/client/ -run TestApplyMultipleItemsWithExecPlugin -v
```
and observe 10 transport creations to apply 10 items (plus a couple others for discovery):
```
before apply
creating transport
creating transport
creating transport
creating transport
creating transport
creating transport
creating transport
creating transport
creating transport
creating transport
creating transport
creating transport
after apply
```

### Anything else we need to know?

This happens because exec auth setup unconditionally sets the GetCert field in transport config here (even if the plugin is only going to return token credentials):

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/58c10aa6eb5adfb1f3aa4d6cb898b8c347ba9e72/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/plugin/pkg/client/auth/exec/exec.go#L303

That makes the transport config uncacheable here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/58c10aa6eb5adfb1f3aa4d6cb898b8c347ba9e72/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/transport/cache.go#L141-L144

Commands like `kubectl describe` and `kubectl apply` repeatedly construct transports when dealing with multiple objects. This poor behavi

enrichment.problem: When using the exec authentication plugin, kubectl opened a new HTTP connection for each object processed (e.g., each manifest in an apply), causing rapid consumption of ephemeral ports and connection failures when many objects were handled.
enrichment.affected: Users running kubectl with the exec auth plugin, especially when applying or describing many resources in a single operation.
enrichment.fix: Modified the client transport handling so that kubectl (and client-go) reuses a single transport/connection when exec auth is active, and stopped the unconditional setting of GetCert in the transport config. This prevents per‑object connection creation and eliminates port exhaustion.
enrichment.impact: Commands that process large numbers of objects (kubectl apply, describe, etc.) no longer fail due to exhausted ports, restoring reliability for CI pipelines, batch deployments, and any workflow that relies on exec‑auth.

To get an equivalent helpful error message in v1.23.5

Make a webhook return a status with code `422` with `Reason` or `Details` not populated, or `Reason` not equivalent to `Invalid`.

enrichment.problem: kubectl versions 1.23 and later show a generic "The request is invalid" message for 422 admission webhook errors that lack a Reason or Details field, losing the detailed context that was displayed in earlier versions.
enrichment.affected: Anyone using kubectl to apply or create resources that trigger admission webhooks returning a 422 status without Reason/Details—e.g., developers, CI pipelines, and operators.

issueContext.title: musl-based DNS resolution will break on v1.25.0 in certain configurations
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

This one involves systemd, DNS, musl, and Kubelet v1.25 😬 👷🏻 🔥 

Starting in v1.25.0, pods running on Kubelets on certain nodes with a FQDN hostname (more on that later) will not be able to resolve DNS queries if they're using musl (e.g. alpine:3.16.2, busybox, etc).

```
# OK
kubectl run debug -it --image docker.io/busybox:1.34.1 --rm=true -- wget www.google.com
kubectl run debug -it --image docker.io/busybox:1.34.1-uclibc --rm=true -- wget www.google.com
kubectl run debug -it --image docker.io/ubuntu:22.04 --rm=true -- /bin/sh -c "apt-get update; apt-get install -y wget & wget www.google.com"

# FAIL
kubectl run debug -it --image docker.io/busybox:1.34.1-musl --rm=true -- wget www.google.com
kubectl run debug -it --image docker.io/alpine:3.16.2 --rm=true -- wget www.google.com
```

Our story starts with systemd. Back in 2020, systemd [started populating](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/17201/files) a "search ." in stub resolvers *if* it detected the hostname to be a FQDN (to solve a separate problem). Check for a static hostname with `hostnamectl`.

In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109441, a change was made to Kubelet to propagate that "search ." into pods (to solve a separate DNS problem). That change landed in `v1.25.0-alpha.1` and appears in `1.25.0`.

Unfortunatey, musl based DNS resolvers struggle with this "search ." EDIT: details in https://github.com/coreos/fedora-coreos-tracker/issues/1287#issuecomment-1232763947

### What did you expect to happen?

musl-based DNS resolvers (depite their other quirks) should continue to function 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

To see if you have a suitable repro node, check your `/etc/resolv.conf` (likely a symlink to `/run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf`.

```
nameserver 127.0.0.53
options edns0 trust-ad
search .                        <--- this is populated by systemd if your hostname is a FQDN
```

enrichment.problem: Kubelet v1.25 propagated the host resolver’s `search .` entry into containers’ /etc/resolv.conf. On nodes with an FQDN hostname, this caused DNS lookups to fail for pods using musl‑based DNS resolvers (e.g., Alpine, musl busybox).
enrichment.affected: Pods on nodes whose hostname is a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) and that use musl‑based containers were unable to resolve DNS queries.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now filters out the host’s `search .` line when generating the pod’s resolv.conf, preventing the problematic entry from being injected.
enrichment.impact: Pods that rely on musl‑based DNS libraries can resolve names again, restoring network connectivity for workloads such as Alpine or busybox‑musl containers that previously failed DNS queries.

issueContext.title: Race between kubelet startup and mounter prepare
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

In GCE cluster startup, kubelet-start (which puts the cluster DNS server into the containerized mounter resolv.conf when the containerized mounter is enabled) race with prepare-mounter-rootfs (which copies the instance resolve.conf into the containerized mounter fs).

This causes domain resolution from the containerized mounter to be flakey.

### What did you expect to happen?

No race to occur.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a GCE cluster with the containerized mounter enabled. Create several nodes. The nameserver in the resolv.conf file in the mounter fs will not be the same.

Note that while it appears the race has existed for a long time, it's only started to manifest around v1.23.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>
v1.23+
</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>
GCE
</details>


### OS version

_No response_

### Install tools

_No response_

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

_No response_

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

_No response_

enrichment.problem: On GCE nodes with the containerized mounter enabled, kubelet startup can race with the mounter’s rootfs preparation. This race leads to the resolv.conf inside the mounter having inconsistent nameserver entries, causing flaky DNS resolution for pods.
enrichment.affected: GCE clusters that enable the containerized mounter; nodes during their startup sequence; pods that rely on DNS resolution.
enrichment.fix: Added synchronization in the kubelet to ensure the containerized mounter setup completes before kubelet adds the cluster DNS entries, eliminating the race condition.
enrichment.impact: Pods on GCE nodes now receive consistent DNS configuration at node startup, preventing intermittent domain‑resolution failures and improving workload reliability.

bugOrRegression.author: akankshakumari393
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: For raw block CSI volumes on Kubernetes, kubelet was incorrectly calling CSI NodeStageVolume for every single "map" (i.e. raw block "mount") operation for a volume already attached to the node. This PR ensures it is only called once per volume per node.

issueContext.title: CSI `NodeStageVolume` called multiple times for same attached volume on same node
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

-  For raw block CSI volumes on Kubernetes, kubelet ends up calling CSI `NodeStageVolume` for every single "map" (i.e. raw block "mount") operation for a volume already attached to the node.

### What did you expect to happen?

[Per CSI spec](https://github.com/container-storage-interface/spec/blob/master/spec.md#nodestagevolume), `NodeStageVolume` should be called once per volume per node:
* More specifically, `This RPC SHOULD be called by the CO when a workload that wants to use the specified volume is placed (scheduled) on the specified node for the first time or for the first time since a NodeUnstageVolume call for the specified volume was called and returned success on that node`.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Create a raw block PVC for a CSI driver
* Create a pod using that PVC
* Create another pod using the same PVC and schedule to the same node
* Kubelet logs will show multiple `blockMapper.stageVolumeForBlock successfully requested NodeStageVolume` for the same PVC.

Example log:

```
Sep 08 23:27:49 node1 kubelet[2820769]: I0908 23:27:49.078408 2820769 csi_block.go:203] kubernetes.io/csi: blockMapper.stageVolumeForBlock successfully requested NodeStageVolume [/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/
kubernetes.io/csi/volumeDevices/staging/pvc-41f58b43-a3eb-4170-a116-98b301a28a67]
...
Sep 08 23:32:54 node1 kubelet[2820769]: I0908 23:32:54.310885 2820769 csi_block.go:203] kubernetes.io/csi: blockMapper.stageVolumeForBlock successfully requested NodeStageVolume [/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/
kubernetes.io/csi/volumeDevices/staging/pvc-41f58b43-a3eb-4170-a116-98b301a28a67]
```

### Anything else we need to know?

Problem appears to be here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a7936658baba02e3ee73324ffe670559f03c188a/pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L1117-L1119

This should first check if "volume is globally mounted" before executing `SetUpDevice`.

enrichment.problem: Kubelet called CSI NodeStageVolume for every raw block volume mapping operation even when the volume was already attached, leading to repeated staging calls per volume per node.
enrichment.affected: Pods that use raw block CSI PersistentVolumeClaims on the same node, as well as the CSI drivers handling those volumes.
enrichment.fix: Added logic in kubelet to track staged raw block volumes and invoke NodeStageVolume only once per volume per node, matching the CSI specification.
enrichment.impact: Eliminates redundant CSI staging RPCs, improving performance and stability for workloads using raw block CSI volumes and preventing potential driver errors caused by multiple staging attempts.

issueContext.title: ANSI escape characters in kubectl output are not being filtered
issueContext.body:
It is a security issue, but after contacting security@kubernetes.io, Tim and the team confirmed that they are comfortable posting it publicly.

#### What happened: 
Kubernetes doesn't sanitize the 'message' field in the Event JSON objects.  
Notice that this is relevant only to JSON objects, not YAML objects. 
By creating new event, we can insert ANSI escape characters inside the "message" field, like:
```
"\u001b[2J\u001b[3J\u001b[1;1H\u001b[m spoofed \u001b[60C\u001b[1;0m. Done"
```


This an example of such JSON request:
```
{
    "apiVersion": "v1",
    "involvedObject": {
        "kind": "Node",
        "name": "node01",
        "uid": "node01"
    },
    "kind": "Event",
    "message": "\u001b[2J\u001b[3J\u001b[1;1H\u001b[m spoofed \u001b[60C\u001b[1;0m. Done",
    "metadata": {
        "name": "spoofEvent",
        "namespace": "default"
    },
    "source": {
        "component": "kubelet",
        "host": "node01"
    },
    "type": "Normal"
}
```

The codes:
`\u001b[2J`   -> Clean the screen and history
`\u001b[3J`   -> Clean the entire screen and delete all lines saved in the scrollback buffer 
`\u001b[1;1H` -> Moves the cursor position to row 1, column 1 (beginning).
`\u001b[m`    -> Set the colors
`\u001b[60C`  -> Move the cursor forward 60 steps
`\u001b[1;1m` -> Set the text colors to white


The result is that the text was spoofed, and we could spoof the events, create hidden events, or hide other events.



#### What you expected to happen: 
The ANSI escape characters will be filtered so they couldn't affect the terminal (i.e. using embeded ANSI colors won't do anything to the terminal).
Or maybe some message that says that you can't use ANSI escape characters.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

1. Run this code:
```

kubectl create -f - <<EOF
{
    "apiVersion": "v1",
    "involvedObject": {
        "kind": "Node",
        "name": "node01",
        "uid":

enrichment.problem: kubectl did not escape ANSI escape sequences present in event messages, allowing malicious JSON events to inject terminal control codes that could clear the screen, move the cursor, or spoof output.
enrichment.affected: All users who run kubectl and view event messages or other resource output that may contain malicious ANSI escape characters.
enrichment.fix: kubectl now sanitizes and escapes terminal special characters in its output, ensuring any ANSI escape sequences are displayed safely rather than being interpreted by the terminal.
enrichment.impact: Users viewing kubectl output can no longer be tricked into unintended terminal actions, mitigating CVE-2021-25743 and improving security for all CLI interactions.

/dir/nested, /dir/nested-vol, /dir/nested.vol, /dir/nested/double, /dir/nested2

        expected: map[nested:{} nested2:{}]

issueContext.title: Admission controllers can cause unnecessary significant load on apiserver
issueContext.body:
Recently we observed high latencies on POST pods on our scalability tests.
For more context see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/22340

It appeared to be throttling related, e.g.:

```
W0302 21:38:28.190204       5 request.go:627] Throttling request took 1.281100127s, request: GET:http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/namespaces/e2e-tests-load-6cqci/limitranges
I0302 21:38:28.191235       5 handlers.go:152] GET /api/v1/namespaces/e2e-tests-load-6cqci/limitranges: (853.53Âµs) 200 [[kube-apiserver/v1.2.0 (linux/amd64) kubernetes/2cf9157] 127.0.0.1:58515]
I0302 21:38:28.193396       5 trace.go:57] Trace "Create /api/v1/namespaces/e2e-tests-load-6cqci/pods" (started 2016-03-02 21:38:26.908795629 +0000 UTC):
[20.412Âµs] [20.412Âµs] About to convert to expected version
[239.558Âµs] [219.146Âµs] Conversion done
[1.282815499s] [1.282575941s] About to store object in database
[1.284377959s] [1.56246ms] Object stored in database
[1.284389884s] [11.925Âµs] Self-link added
[1.284548334s] [158.45Âµs] END
```

As an example look at resource quota admission controller.
In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/20446 there was some fallback added to use lru cache in case of on objects.
However, not what happens if we are sending multiple POST pods at the same time to apiserver.
What happens in Admit() if there are no results in Indexer, we list ResourceQuotas.
But if there are multiple calls at the same time, there can be multiple LISTs before the cache is updated:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/admission/resourcequota/admission.go#L131
But this can cause throttling of these requests.

What we should do is: if there is List() in flight, we should wait until it is finished and lookupCache is updated.

@derekwaynecarr

enrichment.problem: When multiple pods are created concurrently, certain admission controllers (e.g., ResourceQuota) performed LIST requests against the apiserver for each admission check because the cache was empty. This caused a surge of LIST calls, leading to high API server load, throttling, and latency spikes during pod creation.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that create many pods simultaneously and have admission controllers like ResourceQuota enabled; workloads experiencing pod‑creation latency or throttling errors.
enrichment.fix: Admission controller logic was updated to use a fallback LRU cache and avoid repeated LIST operations when the cache is cold, preventing the unnecessary load on the apiserver during high‑throughput pod creation.
enrichment.impact: Reduces API server CPU and request load, eliminates throttling warnings, and restores fast pod‑creation latency even under heavy creation storms, improving overall cluster scalability and stability.

issueContext.title: Regression in winkernel proxier that causes stale load balancing proxy rules
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

There is a regression in v1.24.0 (and above) that causes stale HNS load balancer proxy rules anytime a backend pod is deleted. Each subsequent deletion will leave behind an additional external VIP load balancing rule that references endpoints which no longer exist.

This can cause occasional connectivity issues and timeouts, if a stale load balancing rule is matched and it redirects traffic to an endpoint which no longer exists.

We are under the impression this may have been introduced [here.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/78a507b25647adbf481551c65b900cd817e7a7b3#diff-03419cd19861179be871687a3763ba4440dc39fe688032ecb8e2cbd0efd6f61dR1341) (creds to @sbangari for identifying this.)

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect all load balancing rules created by winkernel proxier (aka HNS load balancer) to be referencing valid backends (aka HNS endpoints)

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Kubernetes cluster v1.24 or higher with Windows nodes.
2. Create a Kubernetes Service with type "LoadBalancer" on Windows.
3. Delete one or more pods of the Service.
4. Observe stale load balancing rule left behind referencing endpoint that was already deleted.

### Anything else we need to know?

This issue can be discovered by establishing multiple connections to the service, after pods were deleted. Some of the requests will fail.

This issue can be monitored using the following script:
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daschott/SDN/patch-1/Kubernetes/windows/debug/networkhealth.ps1

Execute as follows:
`.\networkhealth.ps1 -OutputMode Stdout`

It will print something along the lines of: 
```10/3/2022 8:18:28 PM <my_node_name> @{Problem=Detected 1 stale VIPs <my_service_vip> }```

Another way to inspect this manually is using the following PowerShell:
```powershell
$refs = get-hnspolicylist | select @{Name="VIP"; Expression={$_.Policies.VIPs}}, References | ?

enrichment.problem: The winkernel proxier in kube-proxy leaked HNS load‑balancer proxy rules whenever service backends (pods) were removed. Each deletion left a stale external VIP rule that still referenced the deleted endpoint, causing occasional connection failures and timeouts for services on Windows nodes.
enrichment.affected: Kubernetes clusters version 1.24 and newer that run Windows nodes and use the winkernel proxier for Service load balancing. Any workload that relies on Windows Services can be impacted by the stale rules.
enrichment.fix: The proxier logic was updated to correctly remove obsolete load‑balancer rules whenever service endpoints change, preventing rule leakage.
enrichment.impact: Restores reliable load‑balancing for Services (especially type LoadBalancer) on Windows nodes, eliminating connectivity errors and improving cluster stability for Windows workloads.

issueContext.title: Renaming pod causes duplicate pods if SSA and CSA has been mixed historically
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Through a series of unfortunate events and miscommunication, we've realized we've been using both client-side apply (CSA) and server-side apply (SSA) for a while towards our clusters. Different engineers have used different methods for about a year. It's been fine until about a week ago when we tried to align container names to a certain standard, in a few deployments. We took the deployed manifest, changed the container name, and applied them using `kubectl apply`. Once we did, the deployment spawned two containers: one with the old name and one with the new name (otherwise they were identical). 

Once in this state, we can't seem to get rid of the "extra container" even if we re-deploy different spins on the manifests. The only we found was to delete the entire deployment and re-apply the manifests. This unfortunately leads to downtime since some of the deployments takes a few minutes to be available.

### What did you expect to happen?

We expected the deployment to reflect whatever manifest we applied to the cluster. 

With that said, this episode has lead me to find out about the `managedFields` concept, which I think is in action here somehow. But we've never said to use different field managers, so I am unsure how that feature is supposed to work.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Fist, apply the base using server-side apply:
```console
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply --server-side -f - 
apiVersion: apps/v1                
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  labels:      
    app: my-app  
  name: hello-app
spec:      
  selector:     
    matchLabels: 
      app: my-app
  template:  
    metadata:
      labels:      
        app: my-app
    spec:        
      containers:                  
      - image: strm/helloworld-http
        name: app
        ports:             
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: 
            path: /

enrichment.problem: When using kubectl --server-side with a custom --fieldmanager, fields that were originally set by client-side apply remained owned by the default manager. Those fields could become unmanaged, cause conflicts, appear undeletable, and lead to issues like diff conflicts, duplicate pods, and failed patches.
enrichment.affected: Any kubectl user who mixes client-side and server-side apply, especially when specifying a custom field manager, could experience conflicts or leftover fields.
enrichment.fix: kubectl now automatically migrates ownership of all fields that were set via client-side apply to the field manager specified with --fieldmanager when --server-side is used. This ensures all fields are managed under server-side apply and prevents orphaned field ownership.
enrichment.impact: Users mixing client-side and server-side apply will no longer encounter hidden conflicts or undeletable fields. Resources can be updated cleanly, avoiding extra pods, diff errors, and patch failures, leading to more reliable configuration management.

    print("--

enrichment.problem: The job_controller_job_finished_total metric was sometimes incremented more than once for a single job completion, causing the metric to over-count finished jobs (observed in about 20% of jobs).
enrichment.affected: Users and operators who monitor Job completions via the job_controller_job_finished_total metric, particularly those using indexed Jobs with multiple completions.
enrichment.fix: Adjusted the Job controller logic in kube-controller-manager to ensure the job_finished_total metric is incremented exactly once when a job reaches completion, eliminating the duplicate counting path.
enrichment.impact: Metric accuracy for Job completions is restored, preventing inflated values in Prometheus dashboards, alerts, and any tooling that relies on the job_controller_job_finished_total metric.

issueContext.title: APIServer Tracing crashes with nil pointer exception when egress selector is configured
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

While trying to enable API Server Tracing while using k3s, the API Server component crashes. The only way to avoid this crash is to disable egress selectors in k3s entirely. I originally opened an issue in the k3s repo (see https://github.com/k3s-io/k3s/issues/6254), and we determined that the issue seems to be an assumption that a dialer will always be returned if there's no error, but in this case there's no grpc egress configured so `Lookup` is returning `nil, nil` and causing a panic at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.25.2/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/tracing.go#L106


### What did you expect to happen?

API Server Tracing to function properly.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Please see the linked k3s issue for a repro case; However, I believe the minimal setup for this would be to configure cluster egress without defining a grpc egress selector and then attempting to enable API server tracing.

### Anything else we need to know?

panic stack trace --
```
Oct 11 02:44:12 minikube k3s[10429]: 2022/10/11 02:44:12 <nil>

issueContext.title: Custom resources don't get encrypted in etcd
issueContext.body:
#### What happened:
Trying to encrypt a custom resource in etcd with the following EncryptionConfiguration in kube-apiserver does not lead to encrypted state in etcd.

In this example the custom resource is named "tokens" and belongs to the group "management.cattle.io":

`apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- providers:
  - aescbc:
      keys:
      - name: some-key
        secret: some-secret
  - identity: {}
  resources:
  - tokens.management.cattle.io
- providers:
  - aescbc:
      keys:
      - name: some-key
        secret: some-secret
  - identity: {}
  resources:
  - secrets`

#### What you expected to happen:
Expecting custom resources to be encrypted in etcd if queries e.g. like this:
`etcdctl get /registry/management.cattle.io/tokens/some-token`

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

Activate encryption on the kube-apiserver with a `EncryptionConfiguration` definition on any custom resource and query state in etcd.

#### Anything else we need to know?:
Tested this both with namespaced and non-namespaced custom resources. In both cases encryption does not work.

#### Environment:
- Kubernetes version: v1.20.6
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: Openstack
- OS: flatcar 2765.2.3
- Kernel: Linux host-10-13-39-90 5.10.32-flatcar #1 SMP Tue Apr 27 22:38:30 -00 2021 x86_64 Intel Core Processor (Haswell, no TSX, IBRS) GenuineIntel GNU/Linux
- Install tools: rke version v1.2.9

enrichment.fix: kube-apiserver now accepts CRD resource names in the encryption provider configuration. When a CRD is specified, the API server encrypts its stored objects in etcd using the configured provider.

issueContext.title: Object returned from etcd3 Delete call is inconsistent with what watch returns
issueContext.body:
While working on generalizing tests to somehow better define spec for storage interface (and share them across all implementation of storage.interface - in particular etcd3 and watchcache), I found an unexpected inconsistency in Delete operation in etcd3.

What is happening is that it effectively returns the state of the object from just before the deletion:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.25/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go#L325

However, this is inconsistent with how our watch is working, which is returning the state of the object from just before the deletion, *but* it sets the RV to the moment of deletion (which Delete call isn't doing).


This sounds like a bug to me, but given this is a long-standing behavior we may need to take additional care when fixing this.

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery
/priority important-soon

/cc @liggitt @deads2k @lavalamp @kubernetes/sig-api-machinery-bugs

enrichment.problem: Delete API responses returned a ResourceVersion from before the deletion, while the corresponding delete watch event used the ResourceVersion at the moment of deletion, creating an inconsistency.
enrichment.affected: Any component or client that processes delete responses from the Kubernetes API server—e.g., controllers, operators, and custom scripts—could see inconsistent ResourceVersion values.
enrichment.fix: The delete response now returns the same ResourceVersion that the delete watch event reports (the version at the time of deletion), making both sources consistent.
enrichment.impact: Clients, controllers, and operators that rely on ResourceVersion for consistency checks or watch‑based reconciliation will no longer see mismatched values, reducing bugs and improving reliability of delete‑related workflows.

bugOrRegression.description: Pod logs using `--timestamps` are not broken up with timestamps anymore.
bugOrRegression.author: rphillips
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Pod logs using --timestamps are not broken up with timestamps anymore.

issueContext.title: Pod logs: long lines are corrupted when using timestamps=true
issueContext.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**:

Docker has a hardcoded 16K limit on log line length, which splits lines longer than that into multiple messages in the log file. `ReadLogs` in [logs.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/255a73ffc64d1c4e0f9a378ebf8d0005edfe6962/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/logs/logs.go), however, doesn't account for this when `timestamps` is set to `true` and prints the timestamp in front of every entry in the log file instead of every logical line. This leads to random timestamps appearing in the middle of log lines, potentially breaking the applications that parse these logs.

**What you expected to happen**:

`ReadLogs` inserts timestamps once per logical line, so original log data is preserved. Alternatively, allow `/logs` API to request the logs in a sane format like JSON, which would allow merging the lines back and combining them with the timestamps more intelligently on the application side.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

* Create `foo.yaml`:

      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Pod
      metadata:
        name: log-lines
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: main
          image: busybox
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'while sleep 1; do echo -n ___; for i in $(seq 1 18000); do echo -n A; done; echo ___; done']

 * Start the pod with `kubectl apply -f foo.yaml`
 * Fetch the logs with `kubectl logs log-lines --timestamps`, or using the API (`curl https://…/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/log-lines/log?timestamps=true&container=main`)
 * Observe random timestamps inserted in the middle of the log lines.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
```Client Version: version.Info{

enrichment.problem: When using `kubectl logs --timestamps` on pods that produce log lines longer than Docker's 16KB limit, the kubelet splits the long lines into multiple entries and prefixes each split fragment with a timestamp. This inserts timestamps in the middle of logical log lines, corrupting the log output and breaking parsers.
enrichment.affected: Pods that emit log lines longer than 16KB when the `--timestamps` flag is used, especially on Docker runtimes.
enrichment.fix: The kubelet log reader now reassembles split fragments into the original logical line before adding a timestamp, ensuring timestamps are inserted only once per complete log line.
enrichment.impact: Users can reliably retrieve pod logs with timestamps regardless of line length, preserving log integrity for debugging and downstream log processing tools.

apiVersion: v1

.....

bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Resolves an issue that causes winkernel proxier to treat stale VIPs as valid

issueContext.title: resolve winkernel proxier treating stale VIPs as valid
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

There is an issue on Windows Server 2019 that can cause the kube-proxy call into HNS to delete the load balancer proxy rules to fail.

E.g. 
1. backends of a particular services are all deleted
2. the call to HNS to cleanup the load balancer proxy rules did not succeed
3. the same service get's re-created again in the future and the number of new endpoints matches the number of endpoints that used to exist
4. kube-proxy will think that the old service policy proxy rules that never got deleted is still valid. 

This will lead to in-cluster network failures for traffic passing through Windows Nodes.

### What did you expect to happen?

This case is not handled very well and we should add resiliency to kube-proxy to accommodate such HNS failures.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create Service with 3 backends/pods.
2. Delete 3 pods/backends.
3. <Normally, we would cleanup the policy here, but HNS needs to fail to clean up, which is hard to repro on demand>.
4. Re-create 3 pods/backends.

### Anything else we need to know?

I am not sure if this issue reproduces on Windows Server 2022

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
v1.23 - v1.26
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
Azure, but others should also be impacted.
</details>


### OS version

<details>
Windows Server 2019
</details>


### Install tools

<details>

</details>


### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>

</details>


### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>
Azure CNI, but others would be impacted.
</details>

enrichment.problem: On Windows Server 2019 the kube-proxy winkernel proxier could fail to delete load‑balancer proxy rules in HNS when a service’s endpoints are removed. The stale rules remained marked as valid, so when the service was recreated kube-proxy treated the stale VIPs as active, causing in‑cluster traffic failures on Windows nodes.
enrichment.affected: Kubernetes clusters that run Windows Server 2019 nodes with kube-proxy (winkernel mode). Services whose endpoints are removed and recreated would see stale VIPs cause traffic loss.
enrichment.fix: Added resilience in the winkernel proxier to detect and ignore/delete stale VIP entries when HNS cleanup fails, ensuring that only current service policies are considered valid.
enrichment.impact: Prevents network outages for services running on Windows nodes, restores correct traffic routing, and improves overall reliability of Windows‑based clusters.

issueContext.title: ValidateLabelSelector() allows selectors that error when passed to metav1.LabelSelectorAsSelector
issueContext.body:
#### What happened:

A PDB object with an invalid selector was allowed to be created. This was the root cause of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/98702

#### What you expected to happen:

Invalid selectors to be rejected by API validation, and all selectors that pass `ValidateLabelSelector()` to be able to be passed to `LabelSelectorAsSelector` without error.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

create the following PDB:
```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1beta1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
 name: mypdb
spec:
 minAvailable: 2
 selector:
   matchExpressions:
   - key: name
     operator: In
     values: ["test","bad#value"]
```

Observe events emitted by the controller manager because the selector is invalid:

`4s          Warning   NoPods   poddisruptionbudget/mypdb   Failed to get pods: values[1][name]: Invalid value: "bad#value": a valid label must be an empty string or consist of alphanumeric characters, '-', '_' or '.', and must start and end with an alphanumeric character (e.g. 'MyValue',  or 'my_value',  or '12345', regex used for validation is '(([A-Za-z0-9][-A-Za-z0-9_.]*)?[A-Za-z0-9])?')`

#### Anything else we need to know?:

Tightening this validation function in place will be almost impossible to do compatibly.

A second method that validates the delta will need to be created (or changing the signature of this function to indicate if label values should be validated) . Validation methods that want to tighten validation will have to do so using validation ratcheting:
* apply tighter validation on create
* apply tighter validation on update *only* if the existing object also passes the tighter validation

/sig api-machinery 
as primary owner of the package

There are many APIs that use this validation method. Tagging other sigs with affected APIs:

* admission webhook namespace and object selectors
* statefulset, daemonset, deployment, replicaset, job selectors
* pvc

enrichment.problem: API objects could be created with metav1.LabelSelectors containing invalid label values. These invalid selectors caused runtime errors such as kube‑scheduler panics and controller‑manager failures when the selector was later used (e.g., during affinity matching or PodDisruptionBudget evaluation).
enrichment.affected: Any workload or policy that includes a LabelSelector (pods, Deployments, Services, PodDisruptionBudgets, affinity rules, etc.) could cause scheduler or controller crashes if the selector was malformed.
enrichment.fix: Added strict validation for all LabelSelector fields during API admission. New objects with malformed label values are rejected, while existing objects can still be updated but not newly created with invalid selectors.
enrichment.impact: Prevents cluster‑wide crashes and scheduling failures caused by bad label selectors, improving stability of the scheduler, controllers, and overall API reliability. Users get immediate feedback when they attempt to create resources with illegal label values.

bugOrRegression.description:
'Container `preStop` and `postStart` lifecycle handlers using `httpGet` now
honor the specified `scheme` and `headers` fields. This enables setting custom
headers and changing the scheme to `HTTPS`, consistent with container
startup/readiness/liveness probe capabilities. Lifecycle handlers configured
with `scheme: HTTPS` that encounter errors indicating the endpoint is actually
using HTTP fall back to making the request over HTTP for compatibility with
previous releases. When this happens, a `LifecycleHTTPFallback` event is recorded
in the namespace of the pod and a `kubelet_lifecycle_handler_http_fallbacks_total`
metric in the kubelet is incremented. Cluster administrators can opt out of the
expanded lifecycle handler capabilities by setting
`--feature-gates=ConsistentHTTPGetHandlers=false` in `kubelet`.'
bugOrRegression.author: jasimmons
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Action required: Container `preStop` and `postStart` lifecycle handlers using `httpGet` now honor the specified `scheme` and `headers` fields. This enables setting custom headers and changing the scheme to `HTTPS`, consistent with container startup/readiness/liveness probe capabilities. Lifecycle handlers configured with `scheme: HTTPS` that encounter errors indicating the endpoint is actually using HTTP fall back to making the request over HTTP for compatibility with previous releases. When this happens, a `LifecycleHTTPFallback` event is recorded in the namespace of the pod and a `kubelet_lifecycle_handler_http_fallbacks_total` metric in the kubelet is incremented. Cluster administrators can opt out of the expanded lifecycle handler capabilities by setting `--feature-gates=ConsistentHTTPGetHandlers=false` in `kubelet`.

enrichment.problem: Container lifecycle handlers (preStop and postStart) that used httpGet ignored the scheme and headers fields, preventing use of HTTPS and custom headers and causing incompatibility with probe behavior.
enrichment.affected: Pods that define preStop or postStart lifecycle handlers using httpGet, especially those needing HTTPS or custom headers.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now honors the scheme and headers fields for httpGet lifecycle handlers, allowing HTTPS and custom headers. Handlers configured with scheme: HTTPS that encounter HTTP endpoints fall back to HTTP, emitting a LifecycleHTTPFallback event and incrementing a kubelet metric. The behavior can be disabled via the ConsistentHTTPGetHandlers feature gate.
enrichment.impact: Users can secure lifecycle HTTP calls and pass custom headers, aligning lifecycle handling with probe capabilities. Compatibility is retained via fallback and observability through events and metrics, while admins retain control via a feature gate.

issueContext.title: Command line completion for kubectl plugins
issueContext.body:
<!-- Please only use this template for submitting enhancement requests -->
**What would you like to be added**:
1. When I type `$ kubectl `<kbd>Tab</kbd><kbd>Tab</kbd> I would like to see kubectl plugins in the list of suggested subcommands. For example, if I have installed `kubectl_sniff`, subcommand completions should suggest `sniff`.
2. If the plugin itself also supports command-line completion, `$ kubectl plugin --`<kbd>Tab</kbd><kbd>Tab</kbd> should show suggestions from the plugin command completion.

**Why is this needed**:
Plugins fill in niches in the kubectl workflow, so that they are used rather seldomly. This means that plugin users need to memorize plugin names and their options over long times without using them. Therefore, plugin usefulness would be greatly enhanced by suggesting plugin sub-commands and their options.

enrichment.problem: kubectl shell completion did not suggest installed plugin subcommands, nor provide completion for plugins that support it, forcing users to remember plugin names and options.
enrichment.affected: kubectl users who install and invoke plugins; any workflow that relies on command-line completion for plugins.
enrichment.fix: Shell completion now lists plugin names when appropriate and forwards completion requests to plugins that implement their own completion, enabling `kubectl <Tab><Tab>` to suggest plugins and `kubectl plugin --<Tab><Tab>` to show plugin-specific options.
enrichment.impact: Improves discoverability and usability of kubectl plugins, reducing the cognitive load on users and speeding up workflows that rely on plugins.

issueContext.title: Having two Default StorageClasses should be handled better
issueContext.body:
Presumably this would occur when changing the default from one class to another.  E.g. 

* Class X exists and is marked default
* Class Y is created
* Class Y is marked as default
* Uh oh!!  2 defaults
* Class X is marked as not default
 
At the case in point, when there are 2 defaults, we currently do not assign default values to new PVCs.

We should change this semantic - while there are two, pick one randomly or heuristically.  It's still correct.

Example: Suppose that you have one user changing the default and another user creating a PVC at exactly the same time. What happens?

Depending on network, CPU scheduling, memory allocations, (etc - totally non-deterministic) the API server might see either of those operations first.  The PVC creator will either win the race and get the old default class or it will lose the race and get the new default class.  The difference could literally be whose network has a faster path to the API server.

My point is that whichever one you pick, as long as it is one of those two defaults, it is a correct choice!

Any other FooClass things we do should probably change, too.  I think that's IngressClass and RuntimeClass.

enrichment.problem: When more than one StorageClass is annotated as the default, the DefaultStorageClass admission plugin rejected PVC creation with an error, leaving PVCs without a default class.
enrichment.affected: Clusters where two StorageClasses are simultaneously marked as default, affecting users and workloads that create PersistentVolumeClaims.
enrichment.fix: The admission plugin now selects the most recently created StorageClass among those marked as default instead of returning an error.
enrichment.impact: Clusters that temporarily have two default StorageClasses (e.g., during a default switch or race condition) will no longer fail PVC creation. PVCs will be bound to the newest default class, making default storage class changes reliable and reducing operational disruption.

issueContext.title: Some scheduler goroutines are not tracked in the metric
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

The metric `scheduler_goroutines` is not called in some instances where we initiate routines, like when we call Parallelize

### What did you expect to happen?

We increase the counter every time we create a routine.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

N/A

### Anything else we need to know?

The metric is called `scheduler_goroutines`, but it's already under the `scheduler` system. So the final metric has the name:

`scheduler_scheduler_goroutines`. Maybe we should just call it `goroutines`.

Note that we can't just remove a metric. We need to duplicate and mark the old one as deprecated for a release or two.

### Kubernetes version

<details>
master
</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
N/A
</details>


### OS version

_No response_

### Install tools

_No response_

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

_No response_

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

_No response_

enrichment.problem: The existing `scheduler_goroutines` metric did not capture all goroutine creations in the scheduler (e.g., those started via Parallelize), resulting in incomplete observability of scheduler internals.
enrichment.affected: Users relying on scheduler metrics for monitoring and debugging, as well as metric collection systems.
enrichment.fix: Introduced a new `goroutines` metric in kube-scheduler that replaces `scheduler_goroutines` and counts goroutine usage in additional code paths, providing full coverage. The old metric is retained temporarily for deprecation.
enrichment.impact: Operators and developers now get accurate counts of scheduler goroutine usage, enabling better monitoring, debugging, and capacity planning for the scheduler component.

feature.description:
'Added selector validation to `HorizontalPodAutoscaler`: when multiple HPAs
select the same set of Pods, scaling now will be disabled for those HPAs with
the reason `AmbiguousSelector`. This change also covers a case when multiple HPAs
point to the same deployment.'
feature.author: pbeschetnov
feature.userFacingChange: Added selector validation to HorizontalPodAutoscaler: when multiple HPAs select the same set of Pods, scaling now will be disabled for those HPAs with the reason `AmbiguousSelector`. This change also covers a case when multiple HPAs point to the same deployment.

issueContext.title: Undefined behaviour when selected pods overlap in HPA
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

There are cases when selected by HPAs Pod sets overlap due to misconfiguration:

**Example 1:**

_Deployment A_ (with controlling _HPA A_) has selector:
```
...
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      pod: a
...
```

_Deployment B_ (with controlling _HPA B_) has selector:
```
...
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      pod: b
...
```

And there is a group of Pods with:
```
...
labels:
  pod: a
  pod: b
...
```

**Example 2:**

_HPA A_ and _HPA B_ point to the same deployment.

**As a result**

The same Pods are actuated first by _HPA A_ then by _HPA B_ in an unpredictable way.

### What did you expect to happen?

Instead of ambiguous autoscaling in this case:
- the HPAs actuation should be disabled;
- the problem should be reported to the user through conditions.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Follow [HorizontalPodAutoscaler Walkthrough](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale-walkthrough/) but create two deployments. One with:
```
...
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      pod: a
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        pod: a
        pod: b
...
```
Second is the same but replace selector with `pod: b`.
Autoscale both deployments.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"23", GitVersion:"v1.23.9-gke.2100", GitCommit:"465a69496ef6d60ccf5ed7ff76932ac2f72f0308", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-08-16T09:27:58Z", GoVersion:"go1.17.11b7", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"23", GitVersion:"v1.23.9-gke.2100", GitCommit:"465a69496ef6d60ccf5ed7ff76932ac2f72f0308", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-08-16T09:24:59Z", GoVersion:"go1.17.11b7", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
```

</details>


### Cloud p

enrichment.problem: When two or more HorizontalPodAutoscalers select the same set of Pods—either due to overlapping label selectors or because they target the same Deployment—the autoscaling controller would act on the Pods in an unpredictable order, leading to ambiguous scaling behavior.
enrichment.affected: Clusters where users configure multiple HPAs with overlapping label selectors or multiple HPAs targeting the same Deployment. The affected workloads are the Pods managed by those HPAs.
enrichment.fix: The HPA controller now validates selectors. If it detects that multiple HPAs would manage the same Pods, it disables scaling for the affected HPAs and records a condition with reason `AmbiguousSelector`. This validation also covers the case where different HPAs point to the same Deployment.
enrichment.impact: Prevents undefined or conflicting scaling actions, protecting workloads from erratic replica changes. Users are immediately notified via an HPA condition, making the misconfiguration easier to detect and resolve.

feature.description: Graduate `ServiceIPStaticSubrange` feature to GA.
feature.author: aojea

feature.description: kubeadm: added the "--cleanup-tmp-dir" flag for `kubeadm reset`. It will cleanup the contents of `/etc/kubernetes/tmp`. The flag is off by default.

feature.description: In 'client-go` `SharedInformerFactory` will now support waiting for goroutines during shutdown.
feature.author: pohly
feature.userFacingChange: client-go: SharedInformerFactory supports waiting for goroutines during shutdown

issueContext.title: SharedInformer documentation is missing or hard to find
issueContext.body:
<!-- This form is for bug reports and feature requests ONLY!

If you're looking for help check [Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/kubernetes) and the [troubleshooting guide](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/debug-application-cluster/troubleshooting/).

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/.
-->

**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:
/kind bug


**What happened**:
I cannot find documentation on the correct way to use informers & shared informers. Without guidance, I ended up writing code that called `"k8s.io/client-go/informers/core/v1".NewPersistentVolumeInformer` (and some others). Although I read the docstring of that method, it was only through conversation with a more experienced contributor that I learned I should instead be calling `"k8s.io/client-go/informers".(*sharedInformerFactory).Core().V1().PersistentVolumes().Informer()`

I also had difficulty understanding whether I needed to call `Run()` on each informer, or on the informer factory. The correct answer turns out to be
`"k8s.io/client-go/informers".(*sharedInformerFactory).Start()`
but that was not apparent from the godoc as `Start()` comes from an embedded interface which I didn't notice.

EDIT: Calling `Start()` before creating informers in the factory results in those informers never generating events. I suppose this means that one should never call `Start()` until all informers have been created? Not sure.

**What you expected to happen**:
There should be a doc somewhere that says, "To use a shared informer, make a factory and call `Start()` on it." and that doc should be easy to find.



/sig api-machinery

enrichment.problem: The SharedInformerFactory shutdown did not wait for its internal goroutines to finish, making it hard for applications to achieve a clean, graceful termination of informers.
enrichment.affected: Go programs that use client-go's SharedInformerFactory, especially those that call Stop/Shutdown and need a graceful termination of informer processing.
enrichment.fix: Added support in client-go so that SharedInformerFactory can wait for its goroutines during shutdown, ensuring all informer processing completes before the factory exits.
enrichment.impact: Applications using client-go informers can now safely stop the factory without risking lost events or race conditions, simplifying shutdown logic and improving reliability.

feature.description: Kubernetes is now built with Go 1.19.1
feature.author: palnabarun

enrichment.problem: Kubernetes binaries were built with an older Go version, limiting access to newer language features, compiler optimizations, and security fixes.
enrichment.affected: Developers, CI pipelines, and anyone building Kubernetes from source. Runtime clusters are not directly affected.
enrichment.fix: The build process has been updated to use Go 1.19.1, compiling all components with the newer toolchain.
enrichment.impact: Provides improved compile‑time checks, potential performance gains, and ensures the codebase stays up‑to‑date with upstream Go security patches. No functional changes to clusters, but CI/CD and developers benefit from the updated toolchain.

feature.description: kube-apiserver: `gzip` compression switched from level 4 to level 1 to improve large list call latencies in exchange for higher network bandwidth usage (10-50% higher). This increases the headroom before very large unpaged list calls exceed request timeout limits.
feature.author: shyamjvs
feature.userFacingChange: kube-apiserver: gzip compression switched from level 4 to level 1 to improve large list call latencies in exchange for higher network bandwidth usage (10-50% higher). This increases the headroom before very large unpaged list calls exceed request timeout limits.

enrichment.problem: Large unpaged list API calls experienced high latency due to gzip compression at level 4, causing some calls to exceed request timeout limits.
enrichment.affected: Clients that perform large unpaged list calls (e.g., controllers, kubectl, custom operators) experienced timeouts due to latency.
enrichment.fix: The kube-apiserver now uses gzip compression level 1 instead of level 4, reducing CPU overhead and improving latency for large list calls. This incurs a 10‑50% increase in network bandwidth usage.
enrichment.impact: Improves responsiveness of large list operations and gives more headroom before timeouts, benefiting controllers, CLIs, and any clients that perform extensive list queries. Slightly higher bandwidth consumption may affect network‑constrained environments.

feature.description: A new `DisableCompression` field (default = `false`) has been added to kubeconfig under cluster info. When set to `true`, clients using the kubeconfig opt out of response compression for all requests to the apiserver. This can help improve list call latencies significantly when client-server network bandwidth is ample (>30MB/s) or if the server is CPU-constrained.
feature.author: shyamjvs
feature.userFacingChange: A new "DisableCompression" field (default = false) has been added to kubeconfig under cluster info. When set to true, clients using the kubeconfig opt out of response compression for all requests to the apiserver. This can help improve list call latencies significantly when client-server network bandwidth is ample (>30MB/s) or if the server is CPU-constrained.

enrichment.problem: Clients could not disable HTTP response compression when communicating with the apiserver, leading to unnecessary CPU overhead and higher list call latency on high-bandwidth connections or when the apiserver is CPU‑constrained.
enrichment.affected: Clients that read kubeconfig (kubectl, custom controllers, scripts) and any workloads performing frequent list calls over fast networks or against CPU‑constrained apiserver instances.
enrichment.fix: Added a `DisableCompression` boolean field (default false) to the cluster section of kubeconfig. When set to true, client libraries (e.g., kubectl, client‑go) skip response compression for all apiserver requests.
enrichment.impact: Allows users with ample network bandwidth or CPU‑limited apiservers to reduce list operation latency and lower CPU usage on the server, improving overall responsiveness for large list calls.

feature.description: Logs of requests that were timed out by a timeout handler no longer contain a `statusStack` and `logging error output` fields.
feature.author: Argh4k
feature.userFacingChange: logs of requests that were timed out by a timeout handler will no longer contain a "statusStack" and "logging error output" fields

enrichment.problem: Logs for requests that timed out via a timeout handler included the fields "statusStack" and "logging error output", which are no longer needed and could cause confusion or unnecessary log noise.
enrichment.affected: Operators or tooling that ingest apiserver request logs and rely on the now‑removed fields (statusStack, logging error output).
enrichment.fix: The timeout handler now omits the "statusStack" and "logging error output" fields from the request log entries, simplifying the log output.
enrichment.impact: Log parsers, monitoring tools, or alerting pipelines that expected these fields must be updated; otherwise they will simply see them absent. No functional impact on request handling.
